Your three loans average 63 percent LTV. Is your portfolio really that safe?

Say you hold a $600,000 loan at 75 percent LTV, a $100,000 loan at 55 percent and a $150,000 loan at 60 percent. The simple average is 63.3 percent.

Weighted average LTV multiplies each LTV by its loan balance, adds those up ($595,000), then divides by the total balance ($850,000). The answer is 70.0 percent.

The $600,000 loan is about 71 percent of your balance, so it pulls the number up. Track the weighted figure, not the simple one.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Worked example: three loans of $600,000 at 75 percent LTV, $100,000 at 55 percent and $150,000 at 60 percent have a simple average LTV of 63.3 percent but a balance-weighted average of 70.0 percent.

sources.title: Weighted Average LTV definition
sources.quote: the weighted average of all of the LTVs for such Purchased Mortgage Loans, weighted on the basis of the current Outstanding Principal Balance of such Purchased Mortgage Loans.

posts.text:
What does it mean when a lender is the loss payee on an insurance policy?

A loss payee is the party entitled to the insurance payout if a claim is made. A mortgagee clause entitles a named mortgagee, the lender, to be paid for damage or loss to the property.

Picture a $240,000 loan and a fire that causes $90,000 of damage. Because the lender is named, the insurer pays the lender for that loss, even though the policy is the borrower's. That is 37.5 percent of the balance.

Check that your name is on the policy.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Diagram: a $90,000 fire loss on a property with a $240,000 loan. Because the lender is named as loss payee under the mortgagee clause, the insurer pays the lender for the loss. The claim equals 37.5 percent of the balance.

sources.title: What is a mortgagee clause?
sources.quote: a clause in an insurance contract that entitles a named mortgagee to be paid for damage or loss to the property. | A loss payee is the party who is entitled to the insurance payout if a claim is made. | If your property is damaged while you (the borrower) are paying off the mortgage, the insurance company will pay your mortgage lender for this loss, even though it's covered on your insurance policy.

posts.text:
Flip profits keep shrinking. What does that mean for a lender?

ATTOM reports that the typical gross profit on a U.S. home flip was $60,526 in the second quarter of 2026, down from $71,000 a year earlier. The typical profit margin was 21.5 percent, down from 27.6 percent.

Those figures leave out rehab costs and other expenses, which ATTOM says flipping veterans estimate typically run between 20 percent and 33 percent of after repair value. Gross profit is only the difference between purchase and resale price.

A thinner margin leaves less room for overruns and delays. Stress test the budget and the exit plan before you fund.
posts.alt: ATTOM Q2 2026 flipping data: typical gross profit $60,526 versus $71,000 a year earlier, profit margin 21.5 percent versus 27.6 percent, and rehab and other costs estimated at 20 to 33 percent of after repair value.

sources.title: Home Flipping Profits Continue Gradual Two-Year Decline (Q2 2026 Home Flipping Report)
sources.quote: In the second quarter of 2026, the typical gross profit, the difference between what flippers purchased and sold homes for, was $60,526. | That was down from $66,932 in the previous quarter and $71,000 at the same time last year. | The typical profit margin for a home flipped in the second quarter of 2026 was 21.5 percent, down from 25.7 percent in the previous quarter and 27.6 percent at the same time last year. | (not including rehab costs and other expenses incurred, which flipping veterans estimate typically run between 20 percent and 33 percent of the property's after-repair value)
